                       STATEN CREEK RANCH’S REPLY BRIEF

                                  I.     INTRODUCTION
       As noted in Staten Realty, LLC’s (“Staten Creek Ranch’s,” Party #390) initial brief, the

routes that are supported by parties who have actively participated in this proceeding can be

grouped broadly into three “corridors” based on where they cross the Colorado River:

       •      The “Northern Corridor” routes (Routes 392 and 410) cross the Colorado River
              while paralleling an existing high-voltage transmission line along Segment U3.

       •      The “Central Corridor” routes (Routes 487, 891, and 894) cross the Colorado
              River in close proximity to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks along
              either Segment J11 (Route 487) or Segment J22 (Routes 891 and 894).

       •      The “Southern Corridor” routes (Routes 296, 572, and “Cherokee Creek G”)
              cross the Colorado River close to an existing pipeline ROW along Segment J31.

       Staten Creek Ranch continues to strongly support Routes 392 and 410, both of which

follow a “Northern Corridor” that would avoid running this line well within a mile of Colorado

Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks, cross the Colorado River while paralleling an existing

transmission line, and take a superior path across open, developed land in the north end of


                                               1
 McCulloch County rather than clearing a new 200-foot right-of-way (ROW) through undeveloped,

densely wooded ranchlands like Staten Creek Ranch. Additionally, Staten Creek Ranch remains

unopposed to the Southern Corridor routes, which may not perform as well as those in the Northern

Corridor, but at least mitigate the worst of the Central Corridor routes’ qualitative downsides.

        None of the arguments presented in other parties’ briefs should persuade the Commission

that a Central Corridor route is the correct choice. As detailed in Staten Creek Ranch’s initial

brief, it is undeniable that the Central Corridor routes would substantially and irrevocably damage

the undeveloped, scenic character of the land surrounding Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge

State Parks, as well as Post Oak Falls on the Colorado River. Unable to justify that, many

proponents of the Central Corridor routes simply failed to address impacts to parks and recreation

areas in their briefs—an issue that the Commission is statutorily required to consider. 1 Realizing

the problem, others conveniently focused entirely on the impacts to parks that were quantified in

the Environmental Assessment’s (EA’s) data tables. And because that data does not capture the

impact of placing a transmission line beyond ½ mile from the boundary of a park, some of the

Central Corridor parties even went so far as to claim that routes like Route 894, which roughly

parallels both state parks’ boundaries at a distance of 0.61-1.0 mile along Segments J22-J23-J27

and crosses some of their most scenic vistas, 2 actually perform better than routes in the Northern

and Southern Corridors, which pass by those parks at distances of ~9.5 and ~5.0 miles,

respectively. The Commission should see through those arguments, and discount them.

         Below, Staten Creek Ranch will address that issue in more detail, as well as many other

specific issues raised in other parties’ briefing. What should not be lost in that discussion is that

this isn’t a case that can be decided based entirely on the quantitative performance of the various

routes. Instead, as it has in prior cases, 3 the Commission should place great weight on the

qualitative impacts that this transmission line will have on the character and uses of the land it will

cross, and find that those impacts justify selecting a route that (in this case) performs only

marginally worse on the quantitative factors that the Commission has traditionally considered most

explicitly.

                             II.      ARGUMENT AND AUTHORITIES
        A.       The impacts of the Central Corridor routes on Colorado Bend and Post Oak

                 1.       Proponents of the Central Corridor routes do not address and cannot
                          excuse the impact that those routes would have on Colorado Bend and
                          Post Oak Ridge State Parks.

would cause significant and irreversible harm to the unspoiled views and natural landscape around

Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks along either Segment J11 or Segments J22-J23-

J27. Unable to justify the severe impacts that the Central Corridor routes would have on two

precious and unspoiled state parks, proponents of those routes either completely fail to address

those impacts or conveniently ignore the impact of segments that stay further than ½ mile from

those parks by focusing myopically on the statistics in the EA data tables. This gaping hole in

marginal increases to cost, length, and habitable structure impacts in order to avoid disrupting the

natural beauty and unspoiled character of the area around Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State

Parks by routing this line along a much more compatible corridor for infrastructure.

those parties simply have no way of justifying the impact of running this line directly past two

state parks. That hole in their analysis is more than enough for the Commission to discount their

conclusion that a Central Corridor route is the best option for this line.

Running this line past the already-disturbed viewshed of a community soccer field is simply not

        B.       The marginal quantitative upsides of the Central Corridor routes do not
                 justify placing the line along that corridor.
        While the Commission’s analysis of transmission line routes often focuses on cost, length,

paralleling, and habitable structure impacts, those factors are far from dispositive, as some parties

imply or even openly assert in their initial briefs. Commission precedent is full of examples where

the Commission selected routes that did not perform optimally with respect to those factors (e.g.,

selecting a route that is not the cheapest, shortest, etc.), and it is undeniable that the Commission

is required to engage in a broad routing analysis that involves a comprehensive evaluation of the

facts and circumstances presented by a particular line. 28 And the fact is that in some cases, there

are good reasons for the Commission to select routes that do not perform optimally on the

statistical metrics that usually factor most explicitly into the Commission’s decisionmaking. As

detailed in Staten Creek Ranch’s initial brief, ALJs and the Commission have previously selected

routes that were much longer, much more expensive, and impacted many more habitable

structures in order to avoid material impacts to important parks and unspoiled scenic areas. 29

        One misleading argument along these lines that merits specific attention is the U3

Landowners’ invocation of Docket No. 58276 to support the idea that cost, length, paralleling, and

habitable structure impacts are “override prongs” that should essentially control the Commission’s

routing analysis and displace other, non-quantitative concerns. 30 As an initial matter, the idea of

“override prongs” has no support in Commission precedent. The Commission’s routing evaluation

is based on a comprehensive review of all routing factors, and does not boil down to picking the

shortest, cheapest path. Additionally, while the Commission did find that statistical performance

outweighed aesthetic concerns in Docket No. 58276, the U3 Landowners do not closely examine

the facts underlying that decision, which reveal that the relative performance of the routes in that

proceeding was not comparable to the routes being considered here. The following bullets

compare the statistical performance of the route the Commission selected (Route 26) against the

route the PFD had proposed (Route 28):

       •         The PFD’s Route 28 cost $53.437 M, which was $7.2 M (15.77%) more expensive
                 than Route 26;

       •         The PFD’s Route 28 directly impacted 61 habitable structures, which was 23
                 (60.53%) more than Route 26;

       •         The PFD’s Route 28 was 7.5 miles long, which was 1.77 miles (30.89%) longer
                 than Route 26;

       •         The PFD’s Route 28 paralleled existing ROW and apparent property boundaries
                 for 68% of its length, which was superior to Route 26, which did so for 55% of its
                 length.

58276 demonstrate that the following claim from the U3 Landowners is actually extremely
